book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 5

clue.text: Any activity, such as a dance for the disabled?

parts.note: the formal dance with a band and a floor, the kind you are invited to
game means lame, the sense kept alive in a game leg

explanation.surface: Some pastime or other laid on for disabled people, a dance perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Game meaning lame survives almost nowhere except the phrase 'a game leg', which is why the second half of the answer hides so well. The definition leans on the idiom: a different ball game is a different matter entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom 'a whole new ball game' the phrase stands for any undertaking at all, not just a sport played with a ball.

clue.text: Reduction in total protection of legionary

indicators.note: 'In' puts one thing inside another, so the word before it goes bodily into the middle of the word after.

parts.note: the total at the foot of a column of figures is its sum
a cut in spending is a reduction

explanation.surface: Less money being spent on keeping a Roman soldier safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduction in total' reads as one idea, a shrinking budget, which is why its three words do not look like separate pieces of wordplay. The shield it names is the tall curved rectangle of the shield-wall, not a round buckler.
explanation.definitionFit: A scutum is the shield a Roman legionary carried, so the phrase names his standard protection rather than armour in general.

clue.text: Get over medical officer's U-turn, perhaps

indicators.note: 'Perhaps' offers what stands before it as one possible arrangement rather than the fixed one, which is a loose way of asking for a shuffle and the only instruction here.

parts.note: a medical officer is MO in the services, the possessive s stays in the mix, and the manoeuvre adds its own five letters

explanation.surface: A doctor changing his mind, and the trouble of getting past it.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of 'U-turn' is raw material, letters and all, rather than an instruction to turn anything round: the manoeuvre is being spelt out, not performed. MO is the forces' medical officer, and his apostrophe-s goes into the pile with him.
explanation.definitionFit: To surmount an obstacle is to get over it, the same figurative climb whether the thing in the way is a wall or a difficulty.

clue.text: Child is below insect

parts.note: inf. is the footnote's short form of Latin infra, below — 'see inf.' sends you down the page
the setters' insect of choice, three letters and always at work

explanation.surface: A youngster standing underneath a creepy-crawly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Below' is not telling you where to put anything: it is the footnote abbreviation inf., from Latin infra, and it supplies half the letters. In an across clue nothing could sit below anything in the first place.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is a child at its youngest, the word the law and the nursery both use for one not yet grown.

clue.text: Some jeering about awfully prurient supplier of gin

indicators.note: the first piece goes about, that is around, the reworked letters

parts.note: some of the word jeering: just its first three letters

indicators.note: prurient done awfully, badly, gets its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a lewd gin distiller, picturing jeers aimed at an indecent drinks supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin takes its name and chief flavour from juniper berries, so the tree is its supplier.
explanation.definitionFit: Gin is flavoured with berries from this evergreen shrub, which therefore supplies the spirit's key botanical.

clue.text: Fish taken for a song? Could be a snag

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the haul of fish an angler lands
second meaning: a comic round for several voices
third meaning: a hidden drawback or difficulty

explanation.surface: An angler wonders whether a fish was sold cheaply and suspects some hidden problem.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings: 'for a song' tempts as the idiom for cheaply, but it is a song in its own right, the musical round.
explanation.definitionFit: The one word names an angler's haul, a musical round sung in turn, and a hidden drawback.

clue.text: Devon clinic backs tax on single family

indicators.note: backs is read as goes backwards, so the word for tax is reversed

parts.note: VAT, value added tax, is the British sales tax
I is the Roman numeral one, a single
stock is lineage, the family a person comes from

explanation.surface: A clinic supports a tax on single-parent families.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition joins two senses in one name: Tavistock is a market town in Devon, and the Tavistock Clinic is a famous London psychiatric clinic.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a Dartmoor market town in the county and to a well-known psychotherapy centre, so it serves for either word.

clue.text: Sort of college, little one, with eater?

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and the definition a noun phrase: the setter is naming the compound the word lives in, an electoral college, rather than offering a synonym for the word itself.

indicators.note: To sort a handful of letters is to put them in whatever order you choose, so what follows is raw material rather than a word.

parts.note: the little one of the two ways to write the word just used: coll. is the abbreviation on the letterhead
the word taken at face value, all five letters

explanation.surface: A small college of one kind or another, with somebody to feed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of college' does both jobs at once: it defines the answer, and read again 'sort' is the instruction to rearrange. 'Little one' then asks for the short form of the word standing in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An electoral college is the body of people whose votes actually choose a president, so 'sort of college' names the word that goes in front of it.

clue.text: Quick blow to the instincts

parts.note: a rap on the knuckles is a sharp blow
Freud's id is the unconscious store of instinct and appetite, sitting under the ego

explanation.surface: A quick punch aimed at where somebody's instincts live.
explanation.walkthrough: Freud divided the mind into id, ego and superego, and the id is the store of instinct and appetite — two letters the crossword never tires of. 'Quick' is an adjective, so the answer is one too.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick and rapid are a plain adjective pair — a rapid reply is a quick one — with no shade of meaning between them.

clue.text: Heeding Lent when converted like the Buddha

indicators.note: Something converted has been turned into something else, so the letters in front are to be made into a different word.

parts.note: eleven letters, exactly the count the grid asks for

explanation.surface: Someone who took Lent seriously and came out of it a changed person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Converted' carries its religious sense on the surface — a convert is what Lent might make of you — and its mechanical one in the wordplay. The Buddha's name is a title rather than a name: it means the one who woke up.
explanation.definitionFit: The Buddha is 'the enlightened one', the title meaning exactly that, so the adjective describes him before it describes anybody else.

clue.text: Girl turning head of Mary Lamb

indicators.note: turning the opening pair round swaps them, so the two letters are read the other way

parts.note: the head, or opening, of Mary taken as its first two letters
Elia was the pen name of the essayist Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A girl turns to look at Mary Lamb, the essayist's sister.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Lamb was Charles Lamb's sister, but here 'Lamb' gives his pen name ELIA, from the Essays of Elia; the girl's name is any girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Amelia is a woman's given name, so it fits a clue asking for a girl.

clue.text: Irrespective of other force, the Queen replaces me for opening

indicators.note: one thing replaces another when it takes its place, so the Queen's letters go where the letter for me stood

parts.note: the initial is the opening letter of a word
I is how a speaker refers to me
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's cipher

explanation.surface: The Queen stands in for me at an official opening, whatever else happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' suggests a ceremony, but it is the initial letter of a word; 'me' is I, which gives way to ER.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics, an inertial frame is one where a body moves uniformly unless acted on, independent of any other force.

clue.text: Instrument beheaded is still with us

indicators.note: To behead a thing is to take the head off it, and a word's head is the letter standing at its front.

parts.note: the navigator's instrument for measuring the sun's angle above the horizon
this S stands at the head of that instrument's name and is the letter struck off

explanation.surface: An instrument that has lost its head and is somehow still around.
explanation.walkthrough: A sextant still rides in the lifeboat as a backup for when the satellites fail, so the surface's survivor and the wordplay's instrument are the same object. 'Beheaded' costs one letter, not a whole top half.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extant has not died out: the manuscripts extant are the ones that have come down to us and can still be read.

clue.text: Whisky money for black food

parts.note: rye is the American whiskey distilled from that grain instead of from barley
bread is the old slang for cash, out of the same drawer as dough

explanation.surface: Drink money being spent on something dark to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: Bread and dough are both slang for money, and the setter has picked the one that is also something to eat. The whisky is the American rye, not the Scotch the surface offers.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye bread is dark brown to black beside a wheat loaf, and black bread is the standard English name for it.

clue.text: Water-carrier keeps silence with German agreement in a piece of drill

indicators.note: To keep a thing is to hold on to it, and what a word holds sits inside it rather than beside it.

parts.note: the thing you fetch water in, a pail with a handle
the noise made for silence, spelt the way a library notice spells it
ja is yes in German

explanation.surface: A water-carrier keeping quiet and nodding along in German during square-bashing.
explanation.walkthrough: Drill is cloth as well as parade-ground practice: a stout cotton twill, and this garment is cut from it. Two short scraps go in together, which is why the carrier's six letters come apart so unevenly.
explanation.definitionFit: Drill is the hard-wearing cotton twill that tropical kit is made from, so a garment cut from it is literally a piece of drill.

clue.text: Handled viewers from long street

indicators.note: A thing made from a set of parts is built out of them in whatever order suits, so the words after it are letters rather than a phrase.

parts.note: ten letters, the length the grid wants

explanation.surface: Opera glasses that came from a long road somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handled' reads as dealt with, the way you handle a customer, and means fitted with a handle. 'From' is the only word asking for a rearrangement, which is about as quiet as an anagram signal gets.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorgnettes are eyeglasses on a stick, raised to the eyes rather than worn, so both halves of the definition are literally true of them.

clue.text: Set to mature pointlessly

indicators.note: Without a point means without one of the compass's, so the letter that names a direction is dropped.

parts.note: what a child is told to do: grow up
W is west on the compass card, and it is the point taken away

explanation.surface: Telling somebody to grow up, for all the good it will do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pointlessly' does not mean the growing up is futile; it means the compass point comes out. 'Set' is a noun here, a set of people, though the clue reads as an instruction to somebody.
explanation.definitionFit: A set and a group are the same collection of things considered together: a set of friends is a group of them.

clue.text: Guardian's job? Not democracy, or else I return my oil

indicators.note: 'Or else' holds out the other possibility, so the letters that follow are to be taken in some order other than the one they come in.

parts.note: twelve letters, counting the one-letter word, which is exactly the grid's count

explanation.surface: A threat to hand back somebody's oil unless the newspaper does its job.
explanation.walkthrough: A guardian rules while the heir is under age, a minority in the legal sense, so the question mark covers a definition that is also a dig at the paper. Araucaria set this for the Guardian itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Rule by a minority is the opposite of democracy, and a guardian's job is exactly that: ruling on someone's behalf through their minority.

clue.text: Electrical device that summarises study for the less intelligent?

parts.note: to con a thing is to learn it by heart, the old verb for studying a page closely
dense means slow-witted, so the comparative is the one further along that scale

explanation.surface: A gadget that boils long texts down for people who cannot follow them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Con' for study is an old sense crosswords keep alive — you con a part before you act it — and has nothing to do with swindling. Calling the dim dense is the same metaphor as calling them thick.
explanation.definitionFit: A condenser is the old name for a capacitor, and a condenser is also whatever condenses a text, so both halves of the definition hold.

clue.text: Fellow player makes anagrams

definitions.meaning: the man beside you in the side, playing for the same result
on the surface a hobby; in the answer a description of its own two halves, which are the same four letters in different orders

explanation.surface: A fellow in the side who does anagrams for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no fodder anywhere to shuffle: the clue is telling you that the answer's two halves are anagrams of each other, and that is the whole of the wordplay. Each half runs to four letters, as the enumeration says.
explanation.definitionFit: A team-mate is a fellow player, the person on your own side rather than one of the opposition.

clue.text: See 7
Supplier of tickets for assorted clean vegetables in carrier

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters inside the word for carrier

parts.note: a tray carries plates or drinks

indicators.note: assorted things are mixed up, so the letters of clean and veg are jumbled

parts.note: veg is the everyday short form of vegetables

explanation.surface: Someone serves a mixed salad of clean vegetables on a tray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supplier of tickets' sounds like a box office, but the answer is a high-street holiday booking shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A travel agency books journeys and holidays, issuing rail, air and ferry tickets to its customers.

clue.text: Gold enclosed in tree by fretful Shakespearean beast

indicators.note: Letters put in a word go inside it, with what is left of it standing on either side.

parts.note: the evergreen of the plantation, four letters and a setter's favourite
or is gold in heraldry, the tincture of a gold field
pent is shut in, as in pent-up feelings that cannot get out

explanation.surface: Gold shut up inside a tree, beside an anxious animal out of Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enclosed' looks like the instruction and is a piece of the answer instead — 'in' does the enclosing. The Ghost in Hamlet says his tale would make the hair stand up 'like quills upon the fretful porpentine'.
explanation.definitionFit: Porpentine is Shakespeare's spelling of porcupine, and fretful is the very word his Ghost attaches to the creature.

clue.text: Ran away with new desk — bad!

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of desk are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: an addled egg is a bad, rotten one

explanation.surface: Someone flees from a dreadful new desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' reads as a verdict on the desk, but it means rotten in the sense used of eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: To skedaddle is a jokey American word for running off in a hurry, so the past tense means fled.

clue.text: Hothead changed 25 with a brown shirt

definitions.note: The answer is an adjective and 'a brown shirt' names a person: the Brownshirts were Hitler's SA stormtroopers, so the setter defines the adjective by the men it describes.

indicators.note: What has been changed is no longer as it was, so the letters named alongside are to be rebuilt in another order.

parts.note: the head of HOT, its first letter
the answer at 25 across, whose eight letters join that one in the mix

explanation.surface: A hot-tempered man who changed sides and put on a brown shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hothead' is one word on the page and two instructions underneath it, since the head of 'hot' is its first letter. The Brownshirts were the SA, the party's street fighters, uniformed in brown and broken by Hitler in 1934.
explanation.definitionFit: A Brownshirt was one of Hitler's SA men, named for the uniform, so anything belonging to them is Hitlerian.

clue.text: Bath robe gives some excitement

indicators.note: Giving some of a thing hands over a part and keeps the rest, so only a run of the letters in front is wanted.

parts.note: five letters running on unbroken across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A dressing gown from the spa town that people find thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B lets Bath look like the spa city, and splitting 'bathrobe' into two words hides the run of letters entirely. 'Gives' reads as the sentence's own verb and is half the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A throb is a surge of feeling you can feel in the body — a throb of excitement — so the noun names excitement as a beat.

clue.text: Unexciting river of 7 or…

definitions.note: The two words define separately: the answer is the adjective meaning unexciting, and it is also the name of a river, which is what 'river' is there to tell you.

parts.note: the answer at 7 down, four letters to be re-set

explanation.surface: A river with nothing exciting about it.
explanation.walkthrough: The instruction to shuffle is in the next clue: 'cooked' at 23 down serves both halves of the pair, which is what the dots are for. The Tame runs through Birmingham and joins the Trent.
explanation.definitionFit: Tame means unexciting — a tame ending to a match — and the Tame is a Midlands river, so one word answers both halves.

clue.text: 23 …8 cooked food

indicators.note: Cooked ingredients come out of the pan as something other than what went into it, so the letters are to be rearranged.

parts.note: the answer at 8 down, four letters going into the pan

explanation.surface: Something cooked, to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots carry the sentence on from the clue above, and 'cooked' is the only instruction in the pair — it does the work for both answers. The letters come from another entry, not from this clue's own words.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat is food in the oldest sense of the word — meat and drink meant anything eaten — as well as the flesh on the plate.
